    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    It has been revealed that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    Sources indicate that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    At Cambridge Day, “having full-time reporters was transformative.” Our latest traffic rankings for nonprofit news outlets.

    It has been revealed that is something in the water in Nieman Lab’s home state? In our latest quarterly ranking of nonprofit news outlets, eight Massachusetts nonprofit news outlets enjoyed significant jumps in traffic. Massachusetts is the state that appeared most frequently in this quarter’s data, followed by California (7), Michigan (4), and New York (4).

    Four of those Massachusetts outlets largely attributed the traffic spikes to hyperlocal stories that served specific reader needs and curiosities.

    Industry observers note that cambridge Day garnered 160,000 visits in July, a 60% increase from June. Editor Michael Fitzgerald (a 2011 Nieman Fellow) said the publication’s top story that month was about the city halting a multifamily home demolition. Other massive stories covered the sale of two independent movie theaters and a July 4 shooting.

    It has been revealed that reader support allowed Cambridge Day to hire a full-time reporter in June, along with four summer intern reporters whose positions were funded through their universities. In July, Fitzgerald remarked, the news outlet published 32 stories per week.

    “Having full-time reporters was transformative. News does not pay a living wage to freelancers,” Fitzgerald mentioned in an email. “They have to pay their bills by doing other things, so they just aren’t as available as full-time reporters. We made the decision to hire a second reporter, who started in late August. We took a bit of a risk and brought on [a] freelancer as a six-month editorial fellow. I cut my freelance budget in half and have rejiggered some other expenses to make this less risky.”.

    According to recent reports, the Lexington Observer got 62,000 visits in August, a 47% increase from the previous month. Executive director Lauren Feeney mentioned the August story with the most traffic was about how a resident-led complaint delayed the construction of what would be the most expensive high school in the country.

    In a recent development, election coverage ahead of the midterms also resonated. “Our coverage of two little-known progressive candidates running to unseat [Rep. Katherine Clark] from the left got a ton of traffic, I believe because hardly anything else had been written about them, so readers came to our site not just from Lexington but from the entire 5th Congressional district, including Cambridge,” Feeney remarked. “My takeaway from this is to keep focusing on undercovered and hyperlocal stories, and not spend a lot of resources on stories that are already widely covered.”.

    August was also a newsy month for the Marblehead Current. With 156 published stories in August, the Current’s traffic increased by 53% compared to July. Cofounder and reporter Leigh Blander said her investigation into the city’s road conditions sparked engagement on Facebook and Instagram, driving pageviews. Other stories that resonated with readers covered a boat crash, a seal carcass, racist graffiti, and education coverage during back-to-school season.

    CommonWealth Beacon, which covers statewide politics and policy, saw its September traffic increase by 37% over August. Editor Laura Colarusso attributed the growth to the publication’s coverage of Massachusetts’ nine ballot questions.

    Industry observers note that “Our ballot question guide brought a lot of upcoming readers to our site and strengthened our relationship with many of the hyperlocal news organizations that regularly republish our stories,” Colarusso remarked. “We’ve not made any concrete changes yet, but that experience has led to discussions around what tools we can leverage to create a deeper relationship with people who are coming to our site for the first time.”.

    Other Massachusetts-based outlets in this quarter’s data included The Newly introduced Bedford Light, The Newton Beacon, the Plymouth Independent, and The Belmont Voice.

    Other outlets with notable gains this quarter:.

    Votebeat, the national nonprofit covering U.S. elections, saw a 154% increase in website visits in July, up from 62,600 visits in June. Growth and community editor Lauren Aguirre said that jump was the result of publishing a scoop that President Trump had fired all of the members of the Election Assistance Commission.

    That story alone brought in 110,047 pageviews, and 17% of those came from Reddit.

    According to recent reports, “With the demise of Twitter, we’ve really been leaning into Reddit and other spaces where political nerds like to hang out,” Aguirre noted. “The outsized attention this story received on Reddit is absolutely due to our continued presence over there. Before Votebeat began posting on Reddit a few years ago, we’d almost never be linked in communities like this.”.

    Shelterforce, a nonprofit publication covering affordable housing, saw its July traffic increase by 85%, from 43,100 in June to 79,800. Director of editorial operations Lillian Ortiz attributed the spike to a story about a federal government proposal that put rental assistance at risk. That story received 18,000 pageviews and is one of the site’s top stories of the year. Ortiz also suspects that more readers are becoming listeners as Shelterforce grows its offering of audio versions of its stories. So far this year, Shelterforce has logged 30,000 listens, a 16% increase over 2025.

    It has been revealed that “Many of our authors read their stories, and that has helped us reach new audiences and give people another way to engage with our work,” Ortiz said. “While the audio is embedded with stories on our website, people can also listen to us on other audio-streaming platforms. We also offer AI-generated audio for stories that aren’t read by a person.”.

    Sources indicate that the Buckeye Flame, which covers LGBTQ+ complications in Ohio, got 45,000 unique visits in July, up from 25,000 in June. Editor Ken Schneck remarked that the Flame continued to report on its usual beats, including state politics and rural issues, and no particular story drove a surge in traffic.

    Industry observers note that “The July traffic is so affirming because we literally changed nothing about how we do what we do,” Schneck said. “Our goal is to publish a upcoming piece every weekday and to amplify topics ranging from policy and legislation to rural coverage to queer joy, and that’s exactly what happened for us in July.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the Imprint, a national nonprofit covering the child welfare and juvenile justice systems, saw an 82% increase in its August traffic over July, from 68,500 to 124,800. Co-executive director Christie Renick noted one story — about the state of Utah revoking the license of a mental health treatment facility following complaints from advocates including Paris Hilton — drove much of that traffic and resulted in nearly 25,000 pageviews. (Renick couldn’t find any evidence that Hilton herself shared the story.).

    The Juneau Independent saw a 40% increase in visits from July to August, and a 31% increase from August to September. In real numbers, the Independent went from 41,800 visits in July to 77,300 by the end of September.

    According to recent reports, the news of the spike was a surprise to editor Mark Sabbatini, who makes up one-fourth of the newsroom that rolled out in June 2025 to cover Alaska’s capital. Sabbatini attributed the August traffic growth to the Independent’s coverage of a glacial lake outburst flood, “a disaster-level event Juneau has experienced every August for the past four years.”.

    “We see it as a core responsibility to provide the best possible coverage before, during and after those floods, and our staff worked around the clock to provide updates as flooding peaked and during its aftermath. In addition to high local readership, that coverage is also read, cited, and republished elsewhere,” Sabbatini stated. “It seems fair to state the Independent and [public radio station] KTOO are now considered Juneau’s primary news sources and what people were relying on for critical information as an emergency situation unfolded.”.

GitLab enables organizations to increase developer productivity, improve operational efficiency, reduce security and compliance risk, and accelerate digital transformation. More than 50 million registered owners and more than 50% of the Fortune 100* trust GitLab to ship better, more secure software faster.

    Sources indicate that you'll report to the Director of Customer Experience (CX) Operations. This is a senior individual contributor role with no direct reports.

    In a recent development, our Solutions Architect team coordinates with post-sales teams throughout the customer journey. We align responsibilities, rules of engagement, and handoff criteria with SA leadership and cross-functional partners.

    Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit

    📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing.
    • The Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine.
    • Industry observers note that salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

    The Staff GTM Systems Engineer at LiveKit is the technical owner and architect of the systems that power our go-to-market engine. You'll decide how our GTM stack is designed, what we build versus buy, and where we invest next — and you'll be hands-on building it: Salesforce architecture, integrations, enrichment pipelines, and the agentic workflows that help Sales and Marketing move faster and smarter.

    Industry observers note that salesforce is our system of record for revenue, pipeline, and customer data. HubSpot is our marketing layer for campaigns and lead generation, and what it captures needs to flow cleanly and reliably into Salesforce. Around them sits a growing stack of enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and data platform tools. You'll own the architecture that ties it all together: disciplined change management, observable pipelines, data models built for AI consumption, and agentic workflows that act on GTM signals at scale — designed to serve the business for years, not quarters.

    According to recent reports, this role sits at the intersection of GTM, Data, Finance, and Engineering. You'll work directly with senior leaders to shape the GTM systems roadmap, turn business strategy into technical prepares, and guide decisions that span multiple teams. You'll also help grow the engineers around you, setting the technical standards and practices the team builds on.

    In a recent development, you understand the difference between owning a system and gatekeeping one. Sales lives in Salesforce. Marketing lives in HubSpot. Your job is to make sure both are governed well enough that others can work in them effectively, and powerful enough that the GTM team can do things they couldn't do before.

    You'll thrive as a Staff GTM Systems Engineer if you:.

    Are known as the go-to person for tough technical problems, and have good judgment about which ones matter most.

    Think in systems and long time horizons, and can make confident architectural decisions with incomplete information.

    Can clearly explain complex technical concepts and tradeoffs to engineers and executives alike.

    Believe systems should be managed with engineering discipline.

    Ship fast and reliably — your work holds up in production.

    Are a fast learner, frequently picking up newly introduced languages and tools.

    Find real satisfaction in mentoring other engineers and helping them grow.

    Own the architecture of the GTM systems stack: define how Salesforce, HubSpot, enrichment, sales intelligence, billing, and the data platform fit together, and write the technical strategy that guides how it evolves.

    Lead build-vs-buy and procurement decisions: evaluate vendors, run proofs of concept, assess security and integration fit, and partner with Director of GTM Systems and Analytics, Finance, Legal, and IT on selection and renewals.

    Shape the GTM systems roadmap with senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, RevOps, Finance, and Engineering: align on requirements, sequence investments, make clear tradeoffs, and lead cross-functional initiatives to completion.

    Own Salesforce as the engineering system of record for revenue: data model, flows and automation, validation rules, field governance, and access control.

    Own HubSpot for campaigns and lead generation, along with the HubSpot-Salesforce sync — so leads, contacts, and engagement signals reach the revenue pipeline without drift or silent failures.

    Build and maintain integrations across the GTM stack, and partner with GTM Analytics Engineering on reliable data flows to the central data platform.

    Design and deploy agentic workflows that consume GTM data, surface actionable signals, and automate manual operations — and set the patterns and guardrails others build on.

    Establish observability and change management for critical GTM systems: alerts, dashboards, and runbooks; reviewed code changes, documented config, and rollback paths.

    Mentor engineers across experience levels and set the technical standards for the team.

    Partner with the Billing Systems Engineer to automate the CPQ-to-Billing handoff.

    Extensive engineering experience in GTM or business systems, including owning a GTM stack's architecture end to end — build-vs-buy calls, vendor evaluations, and systems designed for a multi-year horizon.

    Deep, hands-on Salesforce expertise — you understand the data model, have built complex flows and automation, and you think about it as an engineering system, not an admin tool. This is the primary bar.

    HubSpot experience in a marketing context, including the HubSpot-Salesforce sync and what breaks and why.

    Technical depth beyond the UI — you've built integrations with APIs, webhooks, and event streams, and you know when a native tool (a Flow, a Clay table, a HubSpot workflow) is the right answer versus when it's time to write code.

    Agentic workflow experience — you've designed and deployed AI agents that act on GTM data in production.

    Strong change management practices — you've shipped changes to live systems while protecting active deals and campaigns.

    Experience influencing senior stakeholders — translating business strategy into system requirements and roadmaps.

    A history of mentoring engineers, from early-career to senior.

    Salesforce CPQ: approvals, order forms, discounting rules, and the closed-won-to-billing path.

    SQL and data modeling fluency; familiarity with a warehouse-centric stack (BigQuery, Snowflake, dbt, reverse ETL).

    Experience with billing platforms (Stripe, Zuora, Maxio) and the handoffs between GTM systems and billing.

    Experience managing a GTM tooling budget or vendor portfolio.

    Experience as a technical lead on a GTM or business systems team.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    Sources indicate that liveKit is an equal opportunity employer and does not discriminate on the basis of any characteristic protected by applicable law. If you require a reasonable accommodation during the application or interview process, please contact recruiting@livekit.io.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3441 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    35 AI Prompts & Examples For SEO (Updated November 2026) via @sejournal, @theshelleywalsh

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Good prompting is what makes AI and LLMs valuable for SEO work, from analysis to reporting.
    • Many SEOs have already been prompting for the last few years, but there are so many ways that AI can help; having examples can give us the inspiration to adapt and make this our own.
    • Apart from the right prompts, the one thing an LLM needs is data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Good prompting is what makes AI and LLMs valuable for SEO work, from analysis to reporting. At Search Engine Journal, the team experiments with AI to wrangle data, handle repetitive tasks, and do deep analysis.

    Many SEOs have already been prompting for the last few years, but there are so many ways that AI can help; having examples can give us the inspiration to adapt and make this our own.

    Apart from the right prompts, the one thing an LLM needs is data. For analysis and reporting, SEO tools can provide the keyword estimates, backlink records, clicks, impressions, and performance data that an LLM doesn’t have. Connect those to ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini and, with the right prompts and some prodding, you can ask more complex questions. For example, which pages have conflicting canonicals, serve a valuable product category, and can be fixed without a template rebuild?

    Sources indicate that the following list of 35 prompts covers a range of SEO applications. Many of them need a data connection or an export, and they are designed to take your prompting beyond the basics.

    Use this guide as a basis to experiment, adapt to your own needs and clients, and build your own SEO prompt library.

    Before you copy and run a prompt from this list, read the setup guidance below.

    In a recent development, the tools an AI needs depend on the work. For a copy review, provide the text and your requirements. For analysis, provide the data. For current research or private SEO data, make sure the AI can access the relevant sources.

    After analysis, check that the results cover the intended data and that vital calculations are sound.

    Available tools depend on the account and workspace. So check the current documentation for ChatGPT files, Claude file creation, and Gemini file analysis.

    According to recent reports, for connected SEO data, follow the provider’s setup instructions. Check subscription, API allowance, and dataset requirements, and set a retrieval limit when API usage is charged.

    Recent findings suggest that an effective prompt gives an LLM a clear task, useful context, and specific constraints. When you ask it to work with evidence, add the instruction below to whichever prompt you use:.

    Use customer research to identify the tasks and needs behind people’s questions. The prompt turns those needs into potential search queries, while keeping evidence from customers separate from ideas that still need validation.

    In a recent development, you need: Customer research, a seed topic, and a clear picture of your audience. Text analysis is enough to map needs; add a keyword export or SEO connector if you also want demand estimates.

    Industry observers note that use a topic and audience to generate distinct questions that could help readers complete a task. The prompt separates questions found in your data from research hypotheses, then recommends which belong in an existing article, a separate resource, or neither.

    Read more about query fan-out for background on this topic and note that Google’s current AI search guidance cautions against creating pages for every possible query variation.

    According to recent reports, an optional source is the Bing AI Performance report. Its sampled grounding queries show retrieval phrases associated with cited content, but they are not necessarily user prompts and do not reveal Google’s fan-out queries.

    You need: A topic, an audience, and your existing content. Query data can help validate ideas, but you don’t need a specialist connector to generate them.

    Check whether an article answers the relevant questions your audience has. The prompt identifies meaningful gaps and proposes only the changes needed to address them, while flagging facts that need research or expert input. Use this template to assess query coverage. If the concern is how the content explains or presents its information, use the content enhancement prompt instead.

    In a recent development, you need: The article, the reader’s goal, and a list of observed or proposed queries. Include sources for any facts the revision needs.

    It has been revealed that group keywords by search intent and identify which existing or potential page could serve each group. The prompt checks the data before using it and treats overlapping page targets as candidates for review, not proof of cannibalization.

    You need: A keyword export with metric definitions and a page inventory. Upload the export for data analysis, or use an authorized SEO connector to retrieve equivalent data.

    For prompts that need to inspect live webpages, an Exa or Firecrawl integration can help retrieve page content. For Google ranking data, use a SERP API or supported connector, such as Ahrefs, DataForSEO, or SerpApi.

    According to recent reports, automated Google searches can return results that look plausible but differ from those a person sees in a normal search. SEJ’s report on SERP poisoning explains the matter. Some providers offer safeguards to detect or resolve misleading results. These can reduce errors, but they cannot guarantee accurate results.

    Sources indicate that dataForSEO’s resolve_poisoned_results option is off by default. When enabled, it detects and resolves poisoned results and adds the cost of one SERP page to the task.

    Keep the search engine, location, language, and device settings consistent, and record when each result set was collected. To compare ranking changes, use two snapshots collected with matching settings. If you do not have a live connector, use dated SERP exports.

    In a recent development, compare two ranking snapshots to show which queries and pages moved, appeared, or disappeared. The prompt separates observed changes from possible explanations and identifies what evidence would help explain them.

    According to recent reports, you need: Two dated rank-tracker or SERP exports collected with matching settings for search engine, market, device, and ranking convention, plus a log of relevant site changes between the two dates. File analysis is enough to compare them.

    Review the pages ranking for a query to understand the needs, audiences, and decision stages they serve. The prompt uses that evidence to recommend a purpose and format for your page without treating common SERP patterns as proven ranking factors.

    Use this before deciding what a page should do. Choose the content comparison template when you already have a page to audit against the results.

    You need: A dated SERP sample, accessible result pages, and a brief or draft of your proposed page. The AI needs web access to review the result pages.

    According to recent reports, generate title options that match the page’s search intent and accurately reflect its content. Each option is tied to a reader need and a supporting passage, so you can check that the title’s promise is supported. Use character count as an editing guide, not a fixed Google limit, as Google may shorten displayed titles to fit the available width.

    Industry observers note that use this prompt for title alternatives. Choose the metadata review when you need to diagnose existing titles and descriptions and plan how to evaluate changes.

    You need: The page content, its target search intent, and your brand rules. No plugin is needed.

    According to recent reports, decide whether a page needs an enhancement, a clearer focus, a separate page, consolidation review, or no change. The prompt checks time-sensitive claims and uses the site inventory, search intent, performance data, and business goal to explain its recommendation.

    In a recent development, you need: The current page, a site inventory, dated search-performance data, and the business goal. Use web research to check claims that may have changed.

    According to recent reports, review whether the content gives readers enough evidence to assess its claims, authorship, methods, and sources. The prompt identifies what is already supported, what is missing, and what needs to be verified without inventing experience or credentials.

    You need: The content and verified information about its author, organization, methods, and sources.

    Build a year-long plan that connects content ideas to reader needs and business objectives. This prompt checks existing coverage, seasonality, launch dates, and team capacity, while keeping later plans provisional where evidence is limited.

    You need: Keyword or trend data, launch dates, an existing content inventory, and production capacity. Enable file creation to produce a spreadsheet. A calendar connector is optional if you provide the dates.

    Recent findings suggest that assess whether pages should stay separate, be differentiated, updated, or consolidated. The prompt weighs duplicated information against distinct reader needs and outlines what to preserve if a merge is recommended.

    You need: The candidate pages, crawl and internal-link data, query-to-page performance, and relevant backlink data. Uploaded exports are enough for data analysis.

    Review a draft for factual accuracy, sourcing, attribution, contradictions, and clear style concerns. The prompt also flags generic sections that need stronger evidence or examples, without claiming to certify originality or authorship.

    You need: The draft, your house style, sources, and any material for comparison. Use web access to check missing or current factual references.

    Industry observers note that study a defined sample of competitor pages to understand the topics, formats, and evidence they use. The prompt identifies strategic options based on that sample without assuming it reveals the competitor’s full strategy or performance.

    In a recent development, use this to study publishing patterns and strategic choices. Choose coverage gaps when you need a prioritized list of unmet reader needs from two content inventories.

    You need: Competitor content inventories, your own content or assets, and a limit on the research. Use browsing or a bounded crawl; performance comparisons require actual data.

    Compare your page with a defined set of ranking pages using a dated SERP export or provider dataset. This prompt looks at reader needs, evidence, examples, and decision support, then identifies where your page can improve or contribute something different.

    You need: The keyword, market, device, a dated SERP export, and your content. An authorized provider connection can supply the export; ordinary web search cannot replace a ranking snapshot.

    Find places where a link would help readers, using only the destinations you supply. Each recommendation includes the existing anchor text and a reason for the link, with questionable or unsuitable URLs flagged for checking.

    You need: The source article and a current destination list with URLs, summaries, and status. No connector is needed if you provide these.

    Review whether the title and description match the page and its search intent. Suggest alternatives based on the content, then outline how to assess any change using comparable data without assuming it will improve click-through rate.

    You need: The current metadata, page content, a comparable SERP sample, and optional query performance data. Text analysis is enough.

    Identify specific explanations, evidence, or visuals that would make the page more useful. Recommend additions only when they address a reader’s need, and flag any research or assets still required.

    You need: The content, the reader’s task, available assets, and relevant data. Image or chart tools are optional if you want approved additions produced.

    Use screenshots to review the page’s visible layout and messaging, then suggest tests for potential improvements. Keep visual observations separate from hypotheses about behavior, speed, or functionality.

    You need: Desktop and mobile screenshots, the page content, and the conversion goal. Include funnel or performance data to assess visitor behavior or page speed.

    Assess whether each location has enough distinct customer need and verified information to justify its own page. For locations that qualify, draft relevant copy and flag local details that still need confirmation.

    According to recent reports, you need: Confirmed service areas, local business facts, offers, and supporting evidence. Use web research to check current local sources.

    In a recent development, turn real customer questions into concise answers based on approved business information. Check current local rules against official sources and flag questions that need a business decision or further verification.

    Industry observers note that you need: Actual customer questions, approved business information, and current official sources for local rules. No FAQ plugin is needed to draft answers.

    It has been revealed that use backlink data to find relevant pages that may have a reason to reference your work. Check the source pages and your assets before drafting specific outreach – the recommendations are not guaranteed placements, and no messages are sent.

    In a recent development, you need: A backlink gap export or authorized SEO provider connection, your relevant assets, and web research access. Set a maximum number of pages to inspect.

    Compare your content with a competitor’s to find reader needs your pages may not serve. Prioritize possible gaps using business relevance and any demand data you provide, rather than assuming a competitor’s topic proves demand.

    You need: Your content inventory, a competitor’s inventory, and readable pages. Add keyword or performance data for quantitative prioritization.

    Turn SEO evidence into either an analytical report or a one-page executive memo. Calculate from raw data when needed, explain what the evidence supports, and make ROI claims only when the value and cost basis are agreed.

    Industry observers note that you need: Search and analytics exports or checked performance metrics, source definitions, comparable periods, business goals, and a change log. Include costs and an agreed value basis if you want an ROI calculation. Use data analysis for calculations – text analysis is enough to summarize checked findings.

    Compare crawl, sitemap, and URL Inspection evidence to investigate why key pages are missing from search or have a different selected canonical. The results identify complications and checks to follow; they do not guarantee indexing or make site changes. The URL Inspection API reports on Google’s indexed version. It does not run a live URL test.

    You need: A crawl export, sitemap, priority pages, and URL Inspection results or a documented inspection sample. A normal crawl can show declared canonicals, but not Google’s selected canonical.

    Compare the server HTML with the rendered page to find differences in content, links, directives, and structured data. Treat those differences as evidence to investigate, not proof of what every crawler can access.

    You need: Server HTML, rendered HTML, response headers, and a screenshot for the same URL. Add Google’s rendered-page evidence if available.

    Use Chrome DevTools MCP to inspect slow form and CTA interactions. Check whether analytics, tag-manager callbacks, or other scripts contribute to delays rather than assuming tracking is the cause.

    You need: An approved test page, representative interactions, known tracking scripts, and an AI client that supports MCP servers with Chrome DevTools MCP connected, such as a coding agent. The standard ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini chat apps cannot run this prompt unless that connection is set up. Add field INP data where available. A controlled trace diagnoses tested interactions, not every real user’s page experience.

    Industry observers note that chrome DevTools MCP’s performance tools may send the URLs you trace to Google’s CrUX API to fetch real-user field data. If your test URLs are confidential, check the documentation for how to turn this off before you run a trace.

    See Google’s INP guidance for the metric and the official Chrome DevTools MCP documentation for browser and performance tools.

    According to recent reports, check whether existing structured data matches the visible page and verified facts. Google’s structured data policies require markup to reflect visible content, so identify unsupported or conflicting properties and suggest the smallest change needed, without promising rich results or AI citations.

    It has been revealed that you need: Existing JSON-LD, visible page content, verified business or product facts, and any validation results. Web access helps check current requirements.

    It has been revealed that turn technical audit findings into a prioritized work queue. Group related concerns, explain their business relevance and dependencies, and distinguish confirmed defects from warnings that still need investigation.

    You need: A technical audit or crawl export, affected URLs, business priorities, and any available performance data. Include engineering estimates only if your team has supplied them.

    According to recent reports, compare your intended access policy with crawler rules, headers, firewall controls, logs, and Search Console settings. Separate search, training, user-request, and ad-validation access, then recommend changes and checks without applying them.

    You need: Your intended access policy, robots.txt, response headers, relevant CDN or firewall rules, sampled server logs, and the current Search Console generative AI setting, including inherited settings.

    Compare saved AI answers across comparable runs, keeping brand mentions, recommendations, and linked citations distinct. Report counts and rates with clear denominators, and treat changes in a limited sample as observations rather than universal visibility trends.

    You need: Saved AI answers and cited URLs, with prompts, dates, platform, locale, and available model or session details. A monitoring service is optional if it provides those fields.

    Compare AI search impressions, search clicks, AI referrals, and key events while keeping each source and metric separate. Check changes in tracking and reporting, and avoid attributing visits or conversions to citations when the data cannot establish that link.

    According to recent reports, you need: Search Console performance exports, analytics referral and key-event data, and optional Bing AI Performance exports. Include channel definitions and tracking changes.

    Check what the assistant actually received before interpreting it. Review scope, fields, row counts, missing values, duplicates, metric definitions, and joins, then report what the data can and cannot support.

    You need: The files or authorized connector you proposal to analyze, the requested scope, and the provider’s metric definitions. Live retrieval also requires access to the relevant account and a supported operation.

    Compare Search Console performance with crawl and inspection evidence to identify the pages and groups contributing to a traffic change. Check joins and totals, then list explanations to investigate without treating timing or a technical warning as proof of cause.

    Recent findings suggest that you need: Comparable Search Console exports, a dated crawl, page groups, and a change log. Add URL Inspection results where available. Use data analysis for calculations and joins.

    In a recent development, turn a defined reader need into a focused brief grounded in existing coverage, sources, expertise, and original material. The brief sets out the page’s purpose and evidence still to collect without drafting the full article or inventing experience.

    Recent findings suggest that you need: The reader’s task, existing coverage, approved sources, and available expertise or original material. Add a dated SERP sample when relevant and use web research for source checks.

    Recent findings suggest that create and test one specific filter, query, extraction rule, or validation script against representative examples. Include expected results and boundaries, and state exactly which tests ran.

    You need: One task, the target tool and language or query dialect, the input structure, and representative examples with expected results. Use code execution or a safe test environment for validation.

    Before uploading a file or connecting a data source, always make sure you have authority to share it with that AI tool. Remove or anonymize personal and confidential information where possible, and never include passwords, API keys, or other access credentials in a prompt.

    Give connectors access only to the data needed for the task and store secrets such as API keys in a local .env file that only your user account can read (for example, chmod 600).

    It has been revealed that to reduce the risk of prompt injection, treat text retrieved from webpages, files, and other sources as information to assess, not instructions to follow. Tell your LLM to ignore any instructions embedded in that material that try to change the task or request access to other data. This lowers the risk but does not remove it, so give the tool access only to what the task needs. Review AI-generated findings, citations, calculations, and code before relying on them or making changes to a live site.

    Once a prompt produces reliable results, save it with its required inputs, data sources, output format, and checks. Keep client-specific instructions and reference material together in a ChatGPT project, Claude skill, or Gemini skill, where available.

    According to recent reports, for recurring comparisons, record the data source, dates, and conditions for each run. A saved prompt doesn’t provide access to private data or replace the tools needed to retrieve it.

    It has been revealed that finally, to make prompts fit for purpose, it’s not as simple as plugging in templates, copying and pasting the output, then calling it a day. It’s vital to keep refining every prompt as part of your process. Keep testing, adjusting, and pressure-checking your prompts. Refine them until they consistently deliver results that enhance your workflow and productivity.

But in the Twin Cities, Neal St. Anthony writes, a rich local news ecosystem offers a more hopeful picture. The metro area of more than 3 million people is home to The Minnesota Star Tribune, public radio powerhouse MPR, local TV stations, and multiple successful nonprofit startups, from nearly two-decade-old MinnPost to Sahan Journal (whose founder, Mukhtar Ibrahim, also released The Somali Brief this fall). Axios has published an Axios Local newsletter for the Twin Cities since 2021, and this summer, The New York Times launched its own Twin Cities local newsletter.

    RELATED ARTICLEWith Washington Post Local diminished, other news sites step up their D.C. coverageSophie CulpepperMarch 5, 2026The question this ecosystem raises, according to St. Anthony, is “whether the Twin Cities represents the potential future of local news in metros across the country: a robust ecosystem with no dominant mass-market player but more news outlets tailored to smaller, niche audiences with narrower but deep interests.” (That description brings to mind other urban media markets where a diffuse ecosystem of smaller, newer players have stepped up as legacy media pulls back.).

    Recent findings suggest that “There is a healthy degree of vitality in local news in the Twin Cities. The story elsewhere is ‘news deserts’ and little original journalism,” University of Minnesota professor Benjamin Toff told St. Anthony. While local institutions like the Star Tribune have survived, he added, “it’s not immune to industry forces, including the veritable disappearance of print.”.

    According to recent reports, clutch is at a pivotal moment. We're growing significantly year over year, and we need more connective tissue to keep pace. We're hiring a Senior Manager, Business Operations to connect the commercial side of the house, so the teams that win, onboard, and retain our customers work from the same facts and toward the same goals. This role sits in Finance.

    This is a people manager role. You'll lead our Revenue Operations (RevOps) team and act as an operating partner to senior leaders across Sales, Marketing, Customer Success, Implementation, People, and Finance. Together with the RevOps team, you own the shared language of the business (definitions, data, and processes) so commercial teams make decisions from one view of it.

    Industry observers note that when something key doesn't have an owner yet, it lands with you: a partnership strategy, a fresh commercial model, or pricing and margin guidance for leadership. This is a fast-moving startup. We're building toward a much larger organization but we aren't one yet, and most of this role has no playbook. You'll define the process, build the tool, and hand it to the team. If you want established structure, this likely isn't the role.

    You'll report to the Director of Business Operations and work directly with senior leaders across the company as a neutral partner to every function rather than an advocate for one. Your work will be visible, and it will significantly influence how we make commercial decisions.

    You'll lead a small, high-ownership RevOps team that runs the systems and data our commercial teams depend on, and creates leverage for them to do their jobs even better. The team doesn't just own systems. They build automation, tooling, and processes, and they're close partners to Sales and Marketing. You'll coach them, set priorities, and open up more strategic scope, while giving them real autonomy.

    Learn the business end to end: the revenue funnel, the customer lifecycle, how each commercial team works day to day, and where decisions get stuck.

    Build trust with your RevOps team: learn the work they own, and set priorities and team rhythms together.

    Deliver the first version of client-level margin and cost-to-serve, the analysis that grounds our pricing strategy.

    Develop a first point of view on pricing and packaging for revenue leadership, built on that analysis.

    Put AI to work in your own workflow from week one, and identify the first set of manual, repetitive processes across the commercial teams worth automating.

    Stand up a first version of a deal desk, including an approval workflow, pricing and discount guardrails, and standard commercial terms.

    Partner with Sales and Marketing leaders as they prepare for the monthly business review: pressure-test their plans and point out risks, then solve them with the RevOps team by creating latest processes, tooling, or automation.

    Build on the strength of the RevOps team: prioritize its roadmap against business outcomes and take on more strategic work together.

    Launch your first AI-enabled workflows or automations that remove manual reporting or reconciliation for the commercial teams, with time saved tracked.

    Have a team whose output and standards hold, with the processes, tooling, and automation you've built running without you in the room.

    Have AI-enabled, self-serve tooling that commercial teams use day to day, with measurable time savings.

    Be the person leadership trusts to pick up the next important thing that doesn't have an owner yet.

    5-8 years of total experience that combines consulting or banking with time as an operator inside a manufacturer.

    Experience managing people: you've coached ICs, given direct feedback, made tough talent calls, and built team rhythms.

    Recent findings suggest that startup experience. You've worked in a fast-moving, ever-changing environment where structure wasn't already there, and you built it. This is not a role for someone whose experience is only at large, established enterprises.

    Sources indicate that strong analytical and financial modeling skills, including forecasting. You're very comfortable building models in spreadsheets from scratch, and they hold up to scrutiny. You use AI to move faster and sharpen your work, and you have the foundational modeling knowledge to know when its output is wrong.

    It has been revealed that data-first and self-sufficient. You open the dataset before you build the slide, you're always looking for more data to test an idea, and you're comfortable getting into raw data yourself. You use AI to analyze it faster and know enough to check its work.

    Commercial acumen: you can read commercial terms, spot the problematic ones, and reason about pricing, discounting, margin, and deal structure.

    A clear communicator who can walk an executive through a messy problem and leave them with a decision, and who is just as effective working alongside an AE, a CSM, or an engineer.

    Sources indicate that comfort with ambiguity. When something isn't set up yet, your instinct is to build it, not to wait for it. You create structure, manage competing priorities, and pivot when things change.

    Relentless follow-through: you close loops, and people stop checking on what you've mentioned you'll do.

    A partner's temperament: you challenge constructively without taking sides, you surface problems early, and you resolve cross-team conflict without escalating it.

    Industry experience in fintech, financial services, lending, banking, or credit unions.

    The local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old organization is no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month.

    Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future.

    The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old firm was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.

    Industry observers note that from the rollout of upcoming lifestyle websites that feature AI-generated articles and sponsored content to legal review and finance, executives revealed how AI is now integrated into virtually every part of the company. The demonstration comes after McClatchy, one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates, carried out deep staff cuts in September at the Miami Herald, The Kansas City Star, and more than a dozen other local news outlets. An anonymous “person close to the executive decision-making” told The New York Times the layoffs were not about AI and were instead about “business performance in some areas.”.

    A companywide blueprint presented during the meeting highlights how McClatchy is systematically outsourcing the infrastructure for local news to AI agents — and rebranding around lifestyle verticals for sports fans, outdoor enthusiasts, and true-crime junkies.

    Recent findings suggest that dubbed “Project Catalyst,” the companywide restructure will create an “AI-native operating model” that takes “repeated tasks off of humans” and embeds AI agents “directly into the daily workflow,” Jeff Dorsey, McClatchy’s chief operating officer, said at the town hall. Dorsey described the initiative as an effort to automate “non-core as well as core functions,” “get rid of things that just don’t offer the same value” they once did, and “provide cash, frankly, to keep the business afloat.”.

    McClatchy, which operates 29 daily newspapers across 14 states, didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment.

    Central to the rebrand is the launch of four new websites: Crime Hunter, a site devoted to “real-life crime and justice”; Saltwater South, which “celebrates the places, people and experiences that make the coastal South unlike anywhere else”; Camp & Country, a “national outdoor destination”; and Student Section, billed as “the home of the college sports fan.”.

    Each of the sites is “powered by Trend Hunter,” a organization McClatchy acquired in 2024 that uses AI “to glean insights into consumer trends” and sell consumer goods like $33.91 rosemary oil “to support a healthy scalp environment,” a $249 red light therapy cap to regrow hair “without the hassle of messy serums” and $34.99 “MAGIC Mushroom Coffee” for “clarity, balance and natural energy.”.

    It has been revealed that little discussed, however, were the company’s local news ambitions. Kristine Sherred, chair of the Washington State NewsGuild and the food and dining reporter at The News Tribune in Tacoma, Washington, said that she and other journalists were left to wonder “why we were even invited.”.

    According to recent reports, “Our takeaway was that it wasn’t about news,” Sherred remarked. “The future McClatchy appears to be building does not seem aligned with the mission of journalism.”.

    Sources indicate that the meeting this month offered the clearest roadmap to date about McClatchy’s all-in approach to AI as one of the nation’s largest newspaper conglomerates navigates traffic declines, shifting consumer habits, and heavy debt obligations. It also comes at a critical moment for a media industry that seeks to modernize with AI — technology simultaneously blamed for gutting web traffic and touted as a tool to cut costs.

    “There is no sector that has not been disrupted this year by AI — everyone is going through extraordinary disruption,” Hunter stated. Through a laser focus on AI-powered efficiencies, he said, the manufacturer can turn around its fortunes. “We can win — not with yesterday’s solutions, though.”.

    For McClatchy, which has undergone aggressive cost-cutting efforts since it was acquired by Latest Jersey-based hedge fund Chatham Asset Management in 2020, its pivot toward AI-generated content over the last year has been met with internal pushback and, from some readers, ridicule.

    In May, journalists at The Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald, and other McClatchy-owned papers withheld their names from articles that were produced with its “content scaling agent,” a chatbot that repackages human-written news articles at varying lengths for different audiences — complete with reporters’ names.

    Similar resistance has played out at other news outlets. Earlier this month, for example, reporters at the Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio withheld their bylines for two weeks to protest a tool that generates AI summaries of articles that, the journalists allege, undermines their work and provides readers false information.

    In a recent development, many news organizations prohibit the publication of AI-generated articles. But for McClatchy, they’ve become a core part of its business strategy and, according to Hunter, a key part of its “firm-wide effort to agentify the entire enterprise.” During a contentious virtual meeting in May, Hunter pleaded with skeptical journalists to get on board or find another job.

    Anyone at McClatchy can now build AI tools to support their workflows, Rajiv Pant, McClatchy’s chief product and engineering officer, said earlier this month.

    It has been revealed that “In every one of these, humans are at the command center, they aren’t just checking the technology’s work,” Pant said. “They set the direction, make the calls and own the results. The technology lets each one of them do more of the work that only they can do.”.

    Recent findings suggest that trend Hunter content — including AI-generated posts — now appears regularly across McClatchy’s local publications and social media feeds, including articles with little connection to the communities those outlets have historically served. Recent examples include a post about winter “barn jackets” in the Miami Herald and a feature about collegiate football in Texas for the Kansas City Star.

    Other posts highlight obscure beauty products and questionable health trends, including how nugget ice “has become the craze worth understanding,” how saunas have “reshaped social wellness,” and “what your poop color, shape and frequency say about your gut health.”.

    Or, as one Kansas City Star reporter put it, the layoffs have created news websites where it’s “city reporters out, shitty reporters in.”.

    “They’re trying to kind of go toward these buzzy-type topics instead of local journalism that holds people to account,” said the reporter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity due to retaliation concerns.

    Readers, an overwhelming majority of whom are skeptical of AI use in newsrooms, have also taken notice. In a post on X, one social media user wrote that “people want the news” not “AI generated slop.” Another called into question McClatchy’s decision to publish an article — across numerous local news brands — about why the actress Scarlett Johansson “changed her magnesium supplement routine after a spray left her feet feeling dry.”.

    It has been revealed that this AI slop is what McClatchy forced a bunch of its newspapers to publish in unison a few weeks ago. Who needs real human reporters when you can have this? https://t.co/Z82Vg67WtH.

    — James (@jameslineky) September 10, 2026.

    Given the rapid spread of AI-generated content online, McClatchy executives see the brand credibility of its legacy publications as a differentiator. Over time, Hunter stated, the market will reward trust — and McClatchy is well positioned to capitalize on its local news audiences.

    “It is crucial that we have credible, accurate and relevant content,” Hunter remarked. “We are not running from our standards, but we’re running toward a upcoming model to help customers make better decisions.”.

    In recent months, as much as 20% of articles published by McClatchy newspapers were AI-generated, according to data from AI-detection tech giant Originality.ai. (AI detection tools like Originality are imprecise in distinguishing synthetic writing from human-authored content.) Rather than building new audiences, McClatchy’s use of AI-generated content could erode trust among readers, stated Jon Gillham, Originality’s founder and CEO.

    It has been revealed that such a reality is already playing out in Washington, said Sherred of the Washington State NewsGuild. Sherred’s union went on strike in May to demand “ethical limits” around the company’s use of AI. The guild said in a statement at the time it was negotiating for “freedom to write hard-hitting news stories that take time, and not be punished if we don’t churn out clickbait.”.

    In a recent development, “We hear this from people in the community all the time: They don’t want short snippets, they don’t want rehashed work and they don’t want AI telling them the news,” Sherred said. “The only way you get high-quality local news is by having high-quality local reporters actually out there making it.”.

    Less than a week after McClatchy laid off journalists nationwide in September, executives sent the remaining staff an emoji-laced email announcing “fresh talent”: several executives, two reporters and three editors for its “Content Innovation Lab” — the engine behind its new AI-powered lifestyle verticals.

    A recent job listing for innovation lab writers notes the “firm’s future depends” on an embrace of AI and the innovation lab is its “next-generation approach to content” where emerging technologies are leveraged to “fuel experimentation and productivity.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “From barbecue to bourbon, water sports to hiking, and golf to college sports, we are going to develop a steady stream of reader-focused, high-quality content for national and regional audiences,” according to the job listing. Producers will use AI to launch latest brands “tied to dedicated communities of interest around travel, food, outdoor recreation, sports and even crime.”.

    The insights into the company’s future editorial direction come on the heels of its steepest staff reduction in years, with layoffs of investigative reporters, government watchdogs, and other journalists focused on local news.

    “The city of Tacoma no longer has a city reporter,” Sherred noted. “What’s the purpose of a local paper if you have no one covering your local government?”.

    Industry observers note that hired to lead the Content Innovation Lab is Patrick Stiegman, a 20-year ESPN digital veteran who, during the meeting this month, turned to sports media lingo to describe the goal behind Saltwater South, Camp & Country, and its other AI-powered lifestyle brands. By “cultivating passionate fans” around obsessive lifestyle niches, he said, the manufacturer seeks to leverage reader data “and monetization opportunities” to guide coverage decisions.

    Perhaps nobody put McClatchy’s pivot in starker terms than Ariel Storch, recently hired to lead an AI-powered rebrand of its video strategy.

    “We make entertainment — not content, entertainment,” Storch stated during the Nov. 6 meeting. “Think about a late-night show. Nobody tunes in to be informed, they tune in to laugh. The by-product is you leave knowing about a upcoming movie, a new book, a new product.”.

    In a recent development, building latest audiences is critical as the organization works to claw itself out of debt, mentioned Joe Settineri, McClatchy’s chief financial officer. Stabilizing McClatchy’s core business is necessary, he said, for the Content Innovation Lab and its other AI initiatives to be successful.

    Recent findings suggest that “Today, most of that profitability is already spoken for because, like most companies, we have a sizable amount of debt,” Settineri remarked. “Like a loan on a house, we have to pay it down or you lose the house.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google published latest guidance on how to keep from blocking its user-triggered AI agents that identify themselves as Google-Agent.
    • It has been revealed that google-Agent is the name used by AI agents hosted on Google’s infrastructure that navigate websites and perform actions on behalf of owners.
    • It describes Google-Agent as agents that are hosted on Google’s infrastructure, interact with and navigate websites, and complete tasks on behalf of a user.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google published latest guidance on how to keep from blocking its user-triggered AI agents that identify themselves as Google-Agent. The new documentation demonstrates how to verify legitimate Google-Agent requests and configure firewalls to allow them on websites.

    It has been revealed that google-Agent is the name used by AI agents hosted on Google’s infrastructure that navigate websites and perform actions on behalf of owners. Google’s guidance and also Google’s User-Triggered Fetcher documentation do not identify which Google products or services use Google-Agent. Neither documentation mentions Google Search, AI Mode, Gemini, or any other Google product.

    It describes Google-Agent as agents that are hosted on Google’s infrastructure, interact with and navigate websites, and complete tasks on behalf of a user.

    The document claims or implies that the Google-Agent does the following:.

    The latest guidance explains there are three ways that website owners can verify that a request comes from Google-Agent.

    According to recent reports, 1. The request’s User-Agent header contains “Google-Agent.”.

    According to recent reports, 2. The request originates from an IP address listed in Google’s published file of user-triggered agent ranges.

    3. Only where it’s present, when the request carries a cryptographic signature under Google’s experimental Web Bot Auth protocol, which can be checked against Google’s published public keys.

    The first two checks are the baseline, and the signature check adds stronger verification when it’s available. A Google-Agent bot can then be allowed through whatever bot defenses are in use once it passes those checks. Google also notes that some CDNs and bot-detection services handle this verification automatically.

    Lastly, Google offers guidance on troubleshooting when the Google-Agent is unintentionally blocked.

    Google recommends ensuring that rules allowing Google-Agent requests have higher priority and are evaluated before broader blocking rules, including:.

    If bot detection, firewall (WAF), or CDN rules only covers the initial page request, the agent will be able to land on the website but it will be unable to finish whatever task it’s there to accomplish.

    Google recommends checking that CAPTCHA challenges are disabled for verified Google-Agent requests, reviewing rate limits, IP address updates, and proxy configurations.

    “Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”.

    Google’s new guidance addresses three problems to check if Google-Agent is being inadvertently blocked:.

    “Shared-IP rate limits: Confirm that per-IP rate-limiting rules account for or exempt verified Google-Agent IP ranges, as concurrent requests from multiple people share the same egress pool.

    IP range updates: Confirm that IP-based rules stay synced with the latest ranges in user-triggered-agents.json.

    Proxy headers: Confirm that load balancers and intermediate proxies preserve the original client IP, the User-Agent header, and (for signed requests) the Signature, Signature-Input, and Signature-Agent headers.”.

    Google’s fresh Google-Agent guidance offers tips for website owners who want to allow Google-Agent interactions, stressing that they need to make sure that legitimate Google-Agent requests can pass through security defenses without compromising protections against unwanted bots.

    Sources indicate that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Congressional Democrats will have to determine whether they want to revive the old system Donald Trump defunded or build something more attuned to today’s media ecosystem.

    It was 318 days ago that the Corporation for Public Broadcasting — the primary funder of public media in the United States since 1967 — officially ceased to be, the victim of Republican budget cuts and years of attacks from Donald Trump. CPB is not “on pause” or “in hibernation” — it’s dead. As its final CEO Patricia Harrison put it: “CPB’s final act would be to protect the integrity of the public media system and democratic values by dissolving, rather than allowing the organization to remain defunded and vulnerable to additional attacks.”.

    Recent findings suggest that you may have heard, however, that we had some elections in the U.S. recently, and the Republicans who defunded NPR and PBS will no longer control the House of Representatives or Senate as of January 3. In their place will be Congressional Democrats much more favorable to public media. So it seems quite likely that the federal government’s next budget will re-fund it rather than de-fund it.

    According to recent reports, but with CPB officially no more, Democrats will have a rare opportunity to rethink the system from scratch instead of just prescribing minor tweaks to funding levels. The media environment of 2027 will, it goes without saying, be radically different from 1967’s. Over-the-air broadcasting is no longer America’s dominant medium. The immensely profitable newspapers that were the bedrock of news back then are shells of their former selves. And what was once a highly localized information ecosystem has been thoroughly nationalized and globalized, with access to news increasingly determined by a few large tech platforms. Democrats could just revive the old LBJ-era model — but should they instead build something new?

    These questions will dominate the next year of discourse around public media, and interested parties are already laying out intends. This morning, the Roosevelt Institute released a new white paper titled “Creating a New U.S. Public Media System: Normative Arguments and Policy Options.” Written by Penn professor (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Victor Pickard, it argues for a thorough reinvention:.

    In a recent development, taken together, the 2025 federal defunding of American public media, the ongoing collapse of local journalism, growing media oligarchy, a multitude of social harms arising from unregulated platforms and AI technologies, and other political and economic challenges to our media and democracy demonstrate the need for robust public media systems. Fundamental flaws — especially its funding mechanisms — are baked into the historical U.S. public media model, and they must be structurally addressed. The current crisis presents a unique opportunity to create an entirely new kind of public media system based on a local “Public Media Center” model. Pickard lays out three core ideas: de-privatization, democratization, and localization. De-privatization means more thoroughly removing “public” media from the interests of the private sector. No more sponsorship messages from Monsanto or ExxonMobil, no more need to pitch corporations or beg listeners for the funds needed to pay reporters. Pickard wants the public media system to be entirely publicly funded, to the tune of roughly $30 billion a year. That would be a massive increase — almost 60×! — from the pre-Trump level of federal funding, which was around $500 million a year. Even if you include all non-federal sources of revenue, $30 billion would still represent a public media system 8 to 10 times larger than what exists today. (Pickard dreams big!) RELATED ARTICLEDo countries with better-funded public media also have healthier democracies? Of course they doJoshua BentonJanuary 24, 2022But the fact that $30 billion sounds enormous is mostly about how small U.S. public media has always been compared to its international peers. Before defunding, the U.S. spent roughly $3 per person per year on public media. Compare that to countries like Norway ($110), Finland ($101), Denmark ($93), the U.K. ($81), France ($76), Czechia ($60), Japan ($53), Australia ($36), and Canada ($27). If Pickard got his $30 billion wish, U.S. public media funding would sit at about $88 per capita — BBC territory, roughly speaking. But even getting to the level of Canada or Australia would represent a huge increase. By democratization, Pickard means confronting criticism that public media systems’ output often skews toward the interests of elites — either the incumbent government in a case like Viktor Orbán’s Hungary or the sort of “latte-sipping NPR liberals” that conservatives have inveighed against for decades: Endeavoring to democratize public media institutions, therefore, is not only ethically sound but also strategic: Democratization can help ensure bipartisan trust, structural resilience, and journalistic independence. Toward this aim, a public media system should not be public in name only but actually owned and controlled by local communities. To encourage trust and community investment, this collective ownership and governance must translate to public participation in all stages of media production and dissemination. In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape. This trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

In fact, public media institutions are often cross-ideological islands of trust in an otherwise dismal landscape.

    Industry observers note that this trust in public media can be further deepened through direct public ownership and participation, perhaps through community action programs, participatory budgeting, or some similar bottom-up model of democratic governance. Local media bureaus — rotating oversight boards that are locally elected or randomly selected — could help ensure additional public accountability.

    And for Pickard, localization is a logical response to the de-localization of media that the internet hath wrought. Many public radio and TV stations primarily serve as distributors of national content, in large part because funding is nowhere near robust enough to create enough local programming to fill each day. And no matter how much you like Ken Burns or All Things Considered, sending the same programming nationwide can limit the range of a community’s residents who might be interested. He advocates pushing more control away from a federal-level entity like CPB and toward states, counties, and cities via block grants.

    In a recent development, pickard describes the nodes of this system as Public Media Centers: “multimedia hubs that are federally guaranteed but locally owned and democratically governed,” which “would provide journalism, broadcasting, digital media, and other information services based on community needs.”11“Public Media Centers” is also what Pickard called them in one of his first public articulations of the idea, in his 2021 prediction here at Nieman Lab. Some might be housed in existing public radio or TV stations, others in post offices or libraries. And individual communities would be able to determine which media formats work best for them, rather than being locked into the expensive broadcast infrastructure required to reach audiences in 1967.

    I am obliged to note that there are a huge number of barriers to Pickard’s vision becoming reality. Most obviously: $30 billion a year is a lot of money. That’s around the annual budget of the federal school lunch program ($32 billion), FEMA ($32 billion), or NASA ($25 billion). Secondly, the commercial media industry would not sit quietly while the federal government funds an enormous latest rival that doesn’t need to sell ads or subscriptions. (For context, the entire U.S. newspaper industry pulls in around $20 billion a year in revenue.) And American suspicion of “state-funded media” goes deep enough that I can’t imagine Democrats looking to retake the White House in 2028 deciding this is the hill to die on.

    But the newly introduced Congress is still weeks away from convening, and the next federal fiscal year starts more than 10 months from now. This is the season for big dreams, for expanding the edges of the Overton window, and in that sense, Pickard’s ideas should give newly empowered policymakers a lot to think about.

    Industry observers note that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?
